passages.t: King at Hebron, and a message to Jabesh-gilead
passages.happening:
Saul is dead, and the way to the throne seems open. David does not take it. He asks the LORD first: “Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” “Go up,” the LORD answered. Then David asked, “Where should I go?” “To Hebron,” replied the LORD (verse 1).

So David goes to Hebron with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and his men settle with their households in the towns nearby. ‘Then the men of Judah came to Hebron, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah’ (verse 4).

David is told that the men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul, and he sends them a message: “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him. Now may the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness, and I will also show you the same favor because you have done this” (verses 5-6). He ends by telling them that Judah has anointed him king.
passages.hearers:
This is about 1010 BC, soon after Saul's death. Hebron lies in the hill country of Judah, about nineteen miles south of Jerusalem. It was an old town with deep memories: the patriarchs were buried nearby, and Caleb's clan held it. David had prepared the ground. He had married Abigail, the widow of a Calebite, and he had sent gifts from the plunder of the Amalekites to the towns of Judah (1 Samuel 30:26-31).

Anointing with oil set a person apart for an office. Samuel had anointed David privately years before (1 Samuel 16:13). Now his own tribe anoints him in public, and later all Israel will (5:3). In Israel a king needed both God's choice and the people's recognition, and the repeated anointings show the one becoming the other.

The message to Jabesh-gilead is a king's first act of state. Jabesh lay east of the Jordan, and its men had risked their lives to bury Saul, who had once saved their town (1 Samuel 11; 31:11-13). Burying the dead with honor was a sacred duty. David praises their kindness to Saul with the great covenant words, loving devotion and faithfulness: chesed, loyal love that keeps faith, and emet, love that can be relied on. He does not threaten Saul's loyal friends. He invites them to trust the new king.
passages.later:
Hebron was where Abraham buried Sarah, ‘in the cave of the field at Machpelah near Mamre (that is, Hebron)’ (Genesis 23:19), and where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were laid to rest. David's reign begins in the town of the patriarchs.

The pair of words David uses for Jabesh, loving devotion and faithfulness, is the pair God used of himself on Sinai: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).
passages.asks: David asked God where to go even when the road to the throne seemed obvious. Ask what decisions you make without asking, because the answer seems clear. And ask how you treat people who were loyal to someone you opposed.

passages.t: Two kings, and a contest at the pool of Gibeon
passages.happening:
Meanwhile Abner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Saul's son Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim and makes him king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim and Benjamin, the rest of Israel (verses 8-9). Ish-bosheth is forty years old, and he reigns two years. ‘The house of Judah, however, followed David’ (verse 10). David reigns at Hebron seven years and six months (verse 11).

The two armies meet at the pool of Gibeon, Abner's men on one side and David's men under Joab on the other. Abner proposes a contest. “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” “Let them get up,” Joab replied (verse 14). Twelve men from each side step forward, and each seizes his opponent and drives his sword into his side, ‘and they all fell together’ (verse 16). The place is named Helkath-hazzurim. Then the real battle begins, and Abner's men are beaten (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
For the first time Israel has two kings. Abner takes Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines, who now hold the valleys west of the river. The list of lands he rules is more a claim on the north than firm control, and one of the names, read as Asher, is uncertain in the Hebrew.

The numbers raise a puzzle. Ish-bosheth reigns two years, but David reigns at Hebron seven and a half. Some think Abner needed several years to set Ish-bosheth up after the Philistine victory. Others think David stayed at Hebron for some years after the north joined him, before he took Jerusalem.

The name Ish-bosheth means man of shame. First Chronicles calls him Eshbaal, man of Baal. Most scholars think the scribes who copied Samuel replaced baal, which could simply mean lord and was once used even of the LORD, with bosheth, shame, once baal had become fixed as the name of a Canaanite god.

Gibeon lay north of Jerusalem and is identified with el-Jib, where excavations led by James Pritchard in the 1950s uncovered a large rock-cut pool and jar handles inscribed with the town's name. Whether that pool is the one in this story cannot be proven. The contest looks like combat between champions, meant to settle a quarrel without a full battle. Here it settles nothing. All twenty-four die, and the battle comes anyway. Helkath-hazzurim is usually taken to mean field of blades or field of flints, a name that remembers the slaughter.
passages.later:
Chronicles gives Saul's son his other name: ‘Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal’ (1 Chronicles 8:33).

The pool of Gibeon appears again centuries later. Johanan and his men went after Ishmael, who had murdered the governor Gedaliah, and found him ‘near the great pool in Gibeon’ (Jeremiah 41:12).
passages.asks: Twenty-four young men died at a word from their commanders, and nothing was settled. Ask where you have seen people pay for a quarrel that was never theirs. And ask whether there is a contest you are keeping up that only costs others.

passages.t: Asahel, and the sword that devours
passages.happening:
Joab's brothers are there too, Abishai and Asahel. ‘Now Asahel was fleet of foot like a wild gazelle’ (verse 18), and he chases Abner, ‘not turning to the right or to the left’ (verse 19).

Abner tells him to turn aside and take the equipment of some younger man. Asahel will not stop. Abner warns him again: “Stop chasing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” (verse 22). Still Asahel will not turn, and Abner kills him with the butt of his spear. ‘And every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died’ (verse 23).

Joab and Abishai pursue Abner until sunset. The Benjamites gather around Abner on a hill, and he calls down to Joab: “Must the sword devour forever? Do you not realize that this will only end in bitterness? How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” (verse 26). Joab blows the ram's horn, and the fighting stops. Abner's men march all night across the Jordan to Mahanaim. David has lost twenty men, Asahel among them, and Abner three hundred and sixty. Asahel is buried in his father's tomb in Bethlehem (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The first half of the chapter was calm. David asked the LORD and acted on the answer. The second half is violent and confused, and it is driven by commanders, not kings. Abner and Joab make the decisions, and neither Ish-bosheth nor David appears.

The story of Asahel is told slowly. Abner warns him twice, and the narrator repeats the picture of turning to the right or the left. Asahel, swift as a gazelle, will not turn, and he dies. The line about every man pausing at the place where he fell lets a reader feel the weight of it.

Abner knows what this death means. Asahel's brother is Joab, David's commander, and in that world a brother's blood called for revenge. Abner's question at sunset names the tragedy of the whole war. The enemies are kin, and the word he uses for them is brothers. The ram's horn, the shofar, was the signal that told troops to fight or to stop.
passages.later:
The feud does not end here. In the next chapter Joab kills Abner to avenge Asahel, and on his deathbed David reminds Solomon what Joab did: ‘He killed them in peacetime to avenge the blood of war’ (1 Kings 2:5).

Asahel's name heads the roll of David's mighty men in Chronicles: ‘Now these were the mighty men: Asahel the brother of Joab’ (1 Chronicles 11:26).
passages.hard:
Why does David's rise involve so much killing among Israelites?

The text does not hide the cost. The contest at Gibeon kills twenty-four young men for nothing, the battle kills hundreds, and Asahel's death starts a feud. The narrator tells it as tragedy, not triumph, and the chapter's most memorable speech is Abner's lament over brothers killing brothers. David himself is not shown ordering the battle; the commanders drive the violence, and that will keep happening with Joab.

Some readers see the chapter as an honest record of how kingdoms were actually formed in the ancient world, even the kingdom of God's chosen king. Others stress that Scripture describes such violence to expose it, not to approve it. Either way, the book does not suggest that God's purpose for David needed these deaths, and it leaves the question open for the reader to feel.
passages.asks: Abner asked whether the sword must devour forever. Ask where you have seen a conflict go on long after anyone remembered how it began. And ask what it would take for someone to sound the horn that ends it.
